d: Share a controller, wheel, or HOTAS with the other PCs on your network. Both directions at once. Rumble, force feedback, adaptive triggers, lightbar, player LEDs, and speaker audio return to the real hardware. Pair once with a six-digit code. Works on your home network, and across the internet by swapping connection codes with no VPN needed.

Browse the community controller configs on the Steam Workshop and translate the one you pick into a PadForge profile: buttons, sticks, triggers, keyboard and mouse bindings, shift layers, and macros. Anonymous Steam connection, no account. An import report shows what came across clean and what was approximated. Off until you enable it in Settings.

Open a reWASD config or a DS4Windows profile and every binding is listed first, Clean, Partial or Skipped with its reason, then imported as an ordinary PadForge profile. Shift layers, multi-press macros, turbo, toggles, radial menus, gyro and touchpad modes, lightbar colors and adaptive trigger effects come across. Programs a profile would run are named before you accept it.

Logitech, Fanatec, and Thrustmaster wheels driven in their own native protocols: constant force plus spring, damper, inertia, and friction. A Wheel card for rotation range and RPM shift LEDs, and a Centering card that holds the wheel with a spring or with a car’s steering.

Route game rumble and force feedback to any audio output as low-frequency tones. Four voices with per-voice frequency (20–120 Hz) and gain, mono or controller-stereo split, and a frequency sweep to tune your shaker.
A virtual Switch Pro Controller through HIDMaestro, with gyro passed through from your physical pad. Games and emulators that speak Switch see the real thing.

One slot presents a SteamVR left and right hand pair, driven by any controller, keyboard, or motion source you map to it. Haptics return to the device you are holding. PadForge installs the SteamVR runtime itself, with no Steam account. Controls, not positional tracking, and one VR slot at a time.

Sony headphones with a head tracker become a motion source, confirmed on the WH-1000XM5 family. Turn your head to aim or lean, through the same gyro pipeline everything else uses. Found by capability rather than a model list. Rotation only, never position.

Play sound through the DualSense or DualShock 4 speaker. Mirror a Windows output or route a slot’s macro sounds to the pad. DualSense over USB or Bluetooth, DualShock 4 over Bluetooth through its speaker or its headphone jack, with its headset microphone, and the second-model DualShock 4 through its headphone jack on a cable. Pads with haptic actuators but no speaker (Joy-Con, Switch Pro, Steam Controller, Steam Deck) play the sound as a haptic tone, and a Wii Remote through its own speaker.

Crossfeed, a parametric EQ, and a limiter on the DualSense and DualShock 4 audio path, upstream of the encoder. bs2b crossfeed with the six classic presets, Jan Meier, the bs2b default, and a custom cutoff and feed. A graphic EQ you drag into shape or load from an AutoEq parametric file for your exact headphones, six band types. A feed-forward limiter so a boosted band never clips the pad.
Use a MIDI keyboard or pad controller as a mapping source. Notes, CC, pitch bend, and encoders bind like buttons and axes. Same MIDI API as the MIDI virtual output.
One row, any number of inputs, any number of devices. Six combine modes plus a drag-and-drop formula editor. Cross-device chords for free.
Caps Lock for your controller. Hold, Toggle, Latch, Cycle, Sticky, or No Button. Cycle steps a queue of layers with Next and Previous buttons. Per-layer color and emoji. Cross-device activators.

Browser-based gamepad over Wi-Fi. Ten controller layouts, a multi-touch touchpad, and a builder for your own. Up to 16 phones on one PC at once. Vibration API rumble back to each phone. No app install.

Viewers type ! commands in your stream’s chat, and each word is a button on a Twitch Chat row, mapped like any controller. Holds, chords and sequences in one message, turns taken with !claim and approved by viewers or moderators, and the controller drawn on stream as an OBS browser source.
Pin a transparent touchpad window to any monitor and use it as a touchpad input for the assigned DS4 or DualSense slot. Adjustable opacity, size, and position. No phone required.

Map any touchpad (DualSense, DS4, laptop trackpad, phone web touchpad, overlay) to mouse X/Y with per-axis sensitivity and invert, to a virtual analog stick anchored where your finger lands, or to a wedge-thresholded D-pad. Plus the gesture stack: swipes, taps, longpress, pinch, rotate, custom shape templates. Every toggle is per slot.
Local, Player, and World reference frames. Real-world calibration. Cross-device Aim Engage. Tuning saves per pad per slot.

Two Mouse Position sources read where the desktop cursor sits and push a stick, trigger, or button toward it. A per-row Sensitivity dial (0.1 to 5.0) sets the cursor travel for full deflection. Separate from the Mouse Speed sources that read movement. Primary monitor only.

Native 2D art per profile, plus 3D models for Xbox 360, Xbox One / Elite / Adaptive, Xbox Series, DualShock 4, DualSense, DualSense Edge, the Switch Pro pads, the Steam Deck, and both Steam Controllers. Click any button in 3D to record its mapping.
Scaled Radial, Radial, Axial, Hybrid, Sloped Scaled Axial, Sloped Axial. Per-axis anti-deadzone. Custom sensitivity curves with unlimited draggable points.
Full rumble passthrough. HID PID 1.0 for wheels and joysticks. Audio bass rumble synthesized from system audio. Constant force vector.
Seven DualSense trigger modes plus a one-click GameCube preset. Fifteen lightbar modes including audio-pulse, audio-band, Strobe, Battery and Screen Color.

A lighting mode that follows one display: the whole screen or an area of it, as its most common or its average color. A keyboard or mouse whose lights are known one by one spreads the screen across them. HDR displays read against Windows’ SDR white level.
Xbox impulse trigger passthrough on the assigned physical pad. Same data routes to DualSense as Adaptive Trigger Vibration. Audio-bass trigger rumble.

Combo triggers and Custom Expression formulas. Key presses, mouse, scroll, volume, lightbar, rumble, and axis actions that latch, release, and scale. Twelve fire modes, from On Press through Double, Triple, Long, and Short Press to Toggle and Turbo, plus a per-macro shift-layer scope. Cursor actions to recenter the mouse, pin it at a point, or fence it inside a rectangle. Duplicate a macro in place, copy and paste between virtual controllers, or pull every macro from another in one step.

A menu style that types into any Windows program from a controller, in the focused window’s keyboard layout: a grid, two split halves or a daisy wheel, opened by any input or when a text box takes focus. Word suggestions from Windows’ text prediction, and keys that can type through a virtual hardware keyboard.

Steam Input’s hotbar as a menu style: one row of cells run by Show or Hide, Previous, Next and Fire, each on any button, with Steam’s fire modes and its Wrap Around, Hide After Firing and Re-Center Each Time switches.
Watches the foreground window. Switches when a matching app takes focus. Win11-style flyout confirms.
Gyro and accel on UDP 26760. Cemu, Dolphin, Yuzu, Ryujinx all read it. Plug-and-play for any emulator that speaks Cemuhook.
Channel 1-16. CC for axes, Note On/Off for buttons. A real Windows MIDI Services endpoint with no loopMIDI bridge, or an existing port on the legacy MIDI API.

From 60 to 10,000 Hz, 1,000 by default, set in Settings and overridden per profile. The loop sleeps on a high-resolution waitable timer between passes, and above 2,000 Hz the passes due at one wake of Windows’ timer run back to back. Bit-perfect axis passthrough at defaults. Built on SDL3.
HidHide driver-level cloak. Per-device toggles auto-enable for gamepads. Keep Devices Cloaked Between Launches carries the cloak across launches.

t: A keyboard or mouse for PadForge alone
d: Use Only in PadForge moves a USB keyboard or mouse to WinUSB, so Windows stops using it and its keys and buttons reach only your mappings and macros. A precision touchpad does the same through HidHide while PadForge runs. A 15-second Keep prompt and a one-click restore give it back. No key read through it has been confirmed on hardware yet.

In-app Bluetooth pairing. Press SYNC to bond once and reconnect on any button, or hold 1 and 2 for a temporary pairing. Wii Remote, Remote plus Nunchuk, Classic Controller, and Wii U Pro Controller map as pads. Accelerometer and Motion Plus gyro feed the motion pipeline. The IR camera drives an on-screen pointer, and a Balance Board reports weight and lean.

Read NFC tags through a PC/SC contactless reader and fire a macro on a tap. Register and name each tag from the Devices page. Every tag is its own trigger, next to an Any NFC Tag trigger. Media keys map too, and wireless pads show battery charge with an optional idle-disconnect timer.

Register a phrase and speak it to fire a macro. Recognition runs offline with no account and no cloud. The Vosk model ships inside PadForge and unpacks on first use, and Windows’ own recognizer carries the feature until it is ready. Anything the recognizer hears that is not a registered phrase goes to an unknown bucket rather than firing at random.

Both PlayStation Move devices report over Bluetooth, and the PS4-era wand streams over USB as well. The wand carries a gyroscope, an accelerometer, an analog trigger and its illuminated sphere. The Navigation controller carries a stick, a D-pad and its buttons. Motion needs the wand’s own calibration data, which PadForge reads once from a USB dock. There is no camera tracking, so you get rotation and acceleration but never position.
A headset’s pose and its motion controllers become ordinary mapping sources, so what you hold in VR can drive a flat game.
The 6DoF puck reports as a six-axis controller: three translation axes and three rotation axes moving at once, plus its buttons. Games ignore the device class, so PadForge reads it directly.

A repeat action’s rate follows how hard the input is pressed. Pick the analog source it tracks, a trigger or a DualShock 3 pressure axis, and a light press repeats slowly while a full press repeats at the interval.

Flick a stick or a touchpad and the cursor keeps traveling, coasting to a stop on constant-deceleration physics. Momentum Glide sets how far it coasts, and the touchpad adds fling controls for what a fast flick does.

A degree-ranged tilt mode beside the existing rate mode: hold a tilt and the stick holds its deflection, the way Steam’s Joystick Deflection behaves. Full Tilt Range sets the angle that reaches full deflection, and Gyro Recenter re-zeroes the resting grip.
Get notified before a controller dies mid-game, at a percentage you set, with an optional buzz on the pad itself. The same rumble drives identify, which is how you tell several identical pads apart.

Settings checks GitHub for new versions 20 seconds after launch and every 12 hours, downloads the build for your processor, checks it against the SHA-256 GitHub publishes, and replaces PadForge.exe in place. Install with one click or at the next launch, and opt in to the latest dev build if you want fixes first.

Hall effect and analog keyboards report how far each key is pressed, as their own device row: more than 370 models from 101 brands, Wooting, Razer, Keychron and NuPhy among them. Each key is a source at its depth for a trigger, a stick axis or a button. Windows keeps receiving your typing as usual.

Rapid Trigger presses and releases on movement instead of at one fixed point, on any input with depth: analog keys, triggers, sticks, MIDI controls. Toggle latches a button: one press holds it, the next releases it.

Each port of a Bliss-Box adapter names the console controller in it and maps it the way SDL maps that console’s pad. DualShock 2 pressure, rumble, pictures on a Dreamcast VMU, and N64 Controller Pak backup and restore.
Motion Pitch, Yaw and Roll rows give a PlayStation, Nintendo or Valve virtual controller motion from any input. Speed turns it while the stick is held. Angle leans it and levels it on release.
Calibrate a Wii Remote to your screen, four targets and a press of B each, and the crosshair lands where it points, corrected for twist. A Namco GunCon 2 calibrates the same way.

A second web controller address over plain HTTP, behind a ten-character access code, for browsers that refuse the certificate and for tunnels. Web Menus puts a slot’s Touch Grid menus on the phone as tiles.

Bluetooth LE pads, the iCade, serial I-Force wheels with force feedback, DJI RC remotes, clone Xbox 360 receivers, the Ring-Con, light guns, train controllers and arcade I/O boards, plus 286 pads from the community SDL_GameControllerDB.

t: Rumble and lighting in mice and keyboards
d: A mouse or keyboard assigned to a virtual controller takes that controller’s lighting in its own Lights & Sound section, with the same modes a DualSense lightbar has, and a haptic mouse takes its rumble: the Logitech MX Master 4, the SteelSeries Rival 500, 700 and 710, and the Logitech iFeel mice once they run on PadForge’s driver. PadForge lights 1,572 RGB devices over USB by itself, key by key where their lights are known one by one, with per-layer Key Colors, Set Key Colors macros and Map Key Lights. While Synapse, G HUB or GG runs, that maker’s devices light through it, and the ASUS Aura, MSI Mystic Light and Corsair iCUE rows light through those makers’ SDKs.

The interface in 109 languages, 42 of them complete, each listed under its own name. Arabic, Persian, Urdu and Central Kurdish lay it out right to left, while controller drawings and curves keep their left-to-right layout. With no language picked, PadForge follows the Windows display language.

Blind and low-vision players can use PadForge with a screen reader, tested with NVDA. Every control the Tab key reaches has a name the screen reader speaks, in the interface’s language, status messages are read as they happen, and the keyboard reaches chips, tiles, curve points and dialogs. The app looks the same with or without a screen reader.

Driving games’ telemetry as a controller row: speed, RPM, throttle, brake, clutch, handbrake and steering as axes, and the gear as buttons, from Forza, F1, the Codemasters rally games, EA SPORTS WRC, BeamNG.drive, Live for Speed, Project CARS 2, Automobilista 2, the truck simulators, Assetto Corsa and Assetto Corsa Competizione. Map them, start macros with them, or play adaptive trigger effects from them. Custom Formats reads a game PadForge does not know, and Forward to Port passes the packets on to SimHub or another program.

Fan mods that give the Grand Theft Auto games, Red Dead Redemption 2, Skyrim, Fallout 4 and others adaptive triggers send to a program named DSX. PadForge takes its place: their trigger effects, lightbar, player lights and mute light play on the PlayStation controllers on your virtual controllers, with no DSX installed. Mods for DualSenseY, DSZ and the DS4Windows fork that speaks the same protocol work too.
A game that plays a DualSense’s haptics as audio rumbles every rumble pad on that virtual controller, and Bass Shakers follow the haptic track too. A DualSense that plays the track itself keeps it.

The Novint Falcon through Force Dimension’s SDK: the handle as a stick, the grip’s four buttons as buttons, and a game’s rumble and force feedback as force on the handle about a thousand times a second, with a self-centering Joystick feel or an Aim feel that moves like a mouse. Not yet run on a Falcon.

The screens on Logitech’s GamePanel devices, among them the G15, G19, G510 and G13, on the Mad Catz S.T.R.I.K.E. 7 and on a phone running Logitech Arx Control show the profile, a clock, play time, a stopwatch, a picture or a PlayStation controller’s lightbar color, and the keys beside each screen map as buttons. Macros play pictures, switch modes and run the stopwatch. Not yet run on a screen.

A picture, a timer, the time or a lightbar’s color in a window above your game, set from its page in Extras, with no keyboard screen needed. Clicks pass through it while another program is in front, and the keyboard screen macros drive it.

Home replaces the Dashboard: one switch starts the engine, and each virtual controller has a card with a picture of its controller that lights as you press. The services that stood on the Dashboard are tiles on the Extras page, each with a page of its own. A controller’s page has six sections: Mappings, Sticks & Triggers, Rumble & Haptics, Motion & Touch, Lights & Sound, and Macros & Menus. Ctrl+K finds pages, controllers, devices, profiles, settings and actions, and Settings has five groups and a search box of its own. No setting is removed. Checked in page renders and with the NVDA screen reader, and no controller was put through every page by hand.

Spring mode holds a force feedback wheel at center with one strength. Vehicle mode gives the rim the torque a car’s steering puts on it at the car’s speed and grip, from the steering feel model of Balachandran and Gerdes, for a Sedan, a Compact, a Van, a Race Car or the Stanford X1, with the speed from the game’s telemetry or fixed. Release Test measures the wheel with your hands off it and sets the least damping that returns it without overshoot. No wheel has run it yet: every stability and Release Test result comes from a simulated wheel. Over Remote Link only a Logitech, Fanatec or Thrustmaster wheel gets centering.

Up to ten crosshairs over your game, each a click-through window: a cross with a gap, a center dot and a T shape, a circle of 3 to 64 sides, a dot, or a picture of your own, with color, opacity, rotation and an outline. Toggle Crosshair macros show and hide them. A game in exclusive full screen hides them.

A lens like a sniper scope, the whole display zoomed in through Windows’ full-screen magnifier, or a spotlight that darkens the rest, at 1.25 to 16 times, centered on the display, the pointer or the first crosshair. Magnifier (While Held) shows it only while a button is held. A game in exclusive full screen hides the lens and the spotlight.

A Flydigi Apex 4 in DInput mode, Apex 5 or Apex 6 Pro gets adaptive trigger effects and impulse triggers (resistance on the Apex 4 and Apex 5, trigger coil vibration on the Apex 6 Pro), the DualSense haptic track on the Apex 6 Pro’s grip coils, its own lights on the Lighting card, and Controller Screen… for a picture or a GIF on its screen, by cable. No Flydigi pad has run against PadForge yet. The plain Apex 6 is refused.

Hand Held Legend’s SInput protocol, both ways. An SInput pad arrives with its buttons, sticks, triggers, motion, touchpads, battery and rumble, and its haptics play PadForge’s sounds. An Extended slot can be an SInput Gamepad that SDL opens with its motion and both touchpads. No SInput pad has run against PadForge yet, and no game has run on the virtual one.

PadForge ships HIDMaestro 2.3.0, with 344 device profiles. PadForge offers 246 of them: 143 controllers, 51 keyboards and 52 mice. 97 cannot be deployed yet. Six profiles are new: a wired Xbox One S Controller (Model 1708) that Windows’ own Xbox drivers bind, the USB forms of the Nintendo Switch Online Genesis, N64 and SNES pads, and the Joy-Con Charging Grip with the left or the right Joy-Con. No PadForge build has driven the six yet.
